title: Standard State of Nonvolatile Solutions
lead: Activities are measured against a standard state. For a solute in solution, that state is defined by how the solute behaves at infinite dilution.
notes: The book prints no credits for this page.
exercise_notes: The book sets no exercise here; the one exercise is new and AI-written, with an AI answer to compare against.

exercises.source_id: The standard state for a solution is defined in terms of the infinite-dilution behavior
exercises.prompt: The standard state of a solute is a solution of 1 mol/L in which the solute has infinite-dilution properties. Why can no real solution be in this state, and what does an activity coefficient other than 1 tell you about a real solution measured against it?

answer.hint: Ask how close the solute particles are to one another in a real 1 mol/L solution.
answer.solution:
At 1 mol/L the solute particles are close enough to interact, so a real solution of that concentration does not have infinite-dilution properties. The standard state takes the concentration from 1 mol/L and the behavior from a solution so dilute that solute particles never meet, a combination no real solution has. That is why it is hypothetical.

Measured against it, a solute whose particles did not interact would have an activity equal to its concentration over 1 mol/L, with an activity coefficient of 1. Everything the interactions between solute particles do goes into the activity coefficient, so a value other than 1 measures how far the real solution departs from infinite-dilution behavior.
